explanation: Overloaded operators allow you to redefine the behavior of standard operators (like +, -, <<, etc.) for your custom classes, making your code more intuitive and expressive. In real-world programming, this technique is essential for creating user-defined types that behave like built-in types. For example, you might overload the + operator for a Vector class to add two vectors element-wise, improving readability and reducing the need for verbose function calls. Best practices include: only overloading operators when the operation is intuitive and consistent with their built-in meanings (e.g., don't overload + to mean subtraction); use non-member functions for symmetric operators like + or << to ensure they work with implicit conversions; always maintain const correctness to avoid unintended side effects; and prefer overloading as free functions or friends rather than members when appropriate. Common pitfalls include accidentally changing the operator's precedence or associativity (which C++ doesn't allow), creating non-intuitive behaviors that confuse users, or forgetting that operators like . or :: cannot be overloaded. To avoid these, thoroughly document your overloads and test them extensively in various scenarios.
